source.title: Representation-Guided Parameter-Efficient LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Zeguan Xiao; Lang Mo; Yun Chen; Lei Yang; Jie Zhao; Lili Yang; Guanhua Chen

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation; the paper text includes appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a different unlearning method on targeted-knowledge benchmarks and reports target accuracy, but does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The study reports WMDP target accuracies and an MMLU utility constraint. It does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery. TOFU Forget Quality is an oracle-similarity metric, not a direct targeted-knowledge accuracy or recovery measure. The reported representation-energy and orthogonality diagnostics do not test whether forgotten target knowledge can be recovered.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It proposes ReGLU, a LoRA unlearning method built from RILA initialisation and ROL regularisation. It reports only forget-set metrics for its own method and for LoRA baselines (GD, IHL, FILA, VILA): TOFU Forget Quality, and WMDP Bio/Cyber accuracy on Zephyr-7B-beta under an MMLU >=95% constraint. It runs no recovery attack of any kind: no relearning or fine-tuning, no direction ablation or probing of residual knowledge, no quantization, and no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack. So it never asks whether unlearned knowledge is deleted or only hidden. It uses the WMDP benchmark and forget corpus (from an original source) as an evaluation tool. Its WMDP rows compare methods and test no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that ReGLU consistently beats LoRA-based baselines (FILA, VILA) on TOFU and WMDP while keeping model utility, and that its representation-guided initialisation and orthogonal regularisation separate forget and retain representations. Their description of ReGLU as 'robust' refers to subspace-level control, not attack resistance, and no attack evaluation backs it.
record.recipe_differences: ReGLU is a representation-guided LoRA unlearning method using RILA initialization and ROL regularization; it does not implement the recovery attacks or the specified original methods as its tested intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: WMDP forgetting outcomes vary across the tested balance-parameter values and LoRA ranks.

fits_no_version.finding: ReGLU lowers WMDP accuracy on Zephyr-7B-beta with MMLU kept at >=95% of original (chance 25%). GD+ReGLU: Bio 64.7->41.8, Cyber 44.5->28.4. IHL+ReGLU: Bio 49.7, Cyber 33.1. No robustness or recovery check was run.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning-efficacy benchmark result for a new method, with no attack evaluation. It is not evidence on shallow versus deep unlearning.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No recovery attacks are tested. Chance accuracy is not reported, so the WMDP accuracies cannot establish whether target performance is near chance. The MMLU utility result is given only as an aggregate threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out for the 60-row limit. TOFU Forget Quality and the representation-energy/orthogonality diagnostics were not included because they do not directly measure targeted-knowledge accuracy or recovery.

untested.parts: All of A as a claim about robust removal: the study runs no attack, so whether simple attacks recover the knowledge is never tested. The WMDP accuracies are best-of-grid checkpoints under an MMLU >=95% constraint and serve as method comparisons. Only the Cyber values approach the 25% chance level; Bio stays at 41.8 or higher.
All: no relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
All: no activation-direction ablation and no deletion-vs-blocking analysis. The forget/retain energy-ratio and orthogonality diagnostics describe LoRA update geometry, not residual target knowledge.
All: no quantization (all runs in BF16).
All: no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack.

All: ReGLU is called 'robust and precise', but this refers to subspace-level versus parameter-level control of the forget-retain trade-off. The paper doesn't claim or evaluate resistance to recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The merge refused the earlier verdict because the record's own version list and every row (R1-R35, all tagged 'V1') used undeclared ids V1-V6. The reader's version texts map by content to the declared ids: V1 is 'unlearning works / target accuracy' (A), V2 relearning (B), V3 direction ablation or blocking (C), V4 quantization (D), V5 prompt attacks (E) and V6 counter-method resistance (F). Every row keeps exactly one row_fixes item. Each row is linked to 'none', decided from what it measures (method comparisons, ablations, hyperparameter sweeps and a selection criterion), not by position. The untested list covers A-F. No labels are given: the study tests no version, and it is not an original source. Kept from the earlier verdict: relation, tranche, all row states and links, empty labels and missing, and the fits_no_version entry. Changed: (1) the A and F untested wording; F now notes that 'robust' refers to subspace control, not attack resistance. (2) The R3 problem now says the paper doesn't state chance but WMDP is 4-choice (25%). (3) R27 and R32 problems flag unclear sweep settings: D.3 says all WMDP runs used r=32, and the beta=0.5 sweep value of 36.6 doesn't match the Table 2 beta=0.5 configs. (4) The fits_no_version finding adds the IHL+ReGLU numbers. (5) The R35 problem cites Appendix D.4. I read the text in full, through Appendix D.5. A keyword search for relearn, attack, quantiz, jailbreak, recover and probe found no attack evaluation. No instructions to the reader were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Tests unlearning target accuracy and reports a model-utility constraint, but does not test whether attacks recover knowledge.
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis establishing that target knowledge is merely inaccessible rather than removed.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual, or in-context recovery attack.
ReGLU is evaluated for unlearning performance, not resistance to the listed recovery attacks.
